svg.title: Adding a field needs a default to pass. Removing one doesn't need anything.
svg.desc: Backward compatibility checks. Adding a field with a default value is accepted -- a new reader has a default to use for old data missing the field. Adding a field with no default is rejected with a real 409 and a READER_FIELD_MISSING_DEFAULT_VALUE error -- a new reader has nothing to use. Removing a field entirely is also accepted under backward compatibility, since a new reader simply stops looking for it -- an outcome that overturns the naive assumption that removing a field is always the risky change.
svg.text: BACKWARD Compatibility, Tested Directly Against the Registry
Add field WITH a default
surge_multiplier: double = 1.0
ACCEPTED
a new reader has a value to use
for old data that lacks the field
Add field, NO default
payment_method: string
REJECTED -- 409
READER_FIELD_MISSING_DEFAULT_VALUE --
a new reader has nothing to use
Remove a field entirely
pickup_zone removed
ACCEPTED
the naive assumption says this should
fail -- it doesn't. A new reader just stops looking for it.
BACKWARD only ever asks one question:
"can a NEW reader schema make sense of OLD data?"
FORWARD asks the exact opposite question -- and flips both of these outcomes precisely.
The risk was never symmetrical the way it feels
BACKWARD punishes adding a required field -- not removing one.
